extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, examiners, policymakers, and IP scholars analyzing patent-eligibility across jurisdictions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for determining patent-eligible subject matter, with comparative treatment of U.S. case law (Mayo/Alice/Bilski and Federal Circuit decisions) and laws/practices in major jurisdictions (EPC/EPO, Japan, Korea, China, TRIPS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo/Alice two-step framework (U.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze claims under the two-step Mayo/Alice test: (1) determine whether the claim is 'directed to' a patent-ineligible concept (law of nature, natural phenomenon, abstract idea); (2) if so, determine whether the claim recites an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must ask whether the patent-ineligible concept is what the claim is 'directed to' (step one) and, at step two, whether the claim's limitations (individually and as an ordered combination) supply an inventive concept. Cases: Mayo, Alice, DDR Holdings, Enfish, Bascom, Amdocs, CellzDirect/Rapid Litigation. Criticisms noted: some judges viewed Mayo's second-part breadth as unnecessary and worried it discounts post-solution conventional activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed-to inquiry (what the claim is 'directed to')
rubrics_metrics.description: Under step one, identify whether the claim is directed to an ineligible concept or instead to a specific application or improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is 'not enough to merely identify a patent-ineligible concept underlying the claim' — the court must determine whether that concept is what the claim is directed to. Examples: CellzDirect (claims directed to new laboratory technique); Enfish (claims directed to specific improvement in computer memory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept as ordered combination
rubrics_metrics.description: At step two, consider whether the claim limitations, individually and as an ordered combination, provide an 'inventive concept' beyond generic computer/known components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found eligibility where the ordered combination recites something more than generic components (e.g., Bascom's remote installation with customizable features; Amdocs' distributed architecture and specific computer code enhancing records). The ordered-combination analysis can rescue claims that are otherwise abstract when taken element-by-element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of a technological solution to a technological problem (computer-related inventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that provide a technological solution to a problem specifically arising in the realm of computer networks/technology are more likely to be patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DDR Holdings found eligibility where the claimed webpage-generation system was 'necessarily rooted in computer technology' to overcome a computer-network-specific problem. Enfish found claims eligible as a specific improvement to how computers operate. The 'technological solution' framing distinguishes improvements in computer technology from abstract business practices merely implemented on a computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific, tangible application moves through §101 filter
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are directed to a specific, tangible application (not merely an abstract idea) are more likely to pass the §101 coarse eligibility filter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classen held that claims to administering vaccines according to a determined schedule were directed to a specific, tangible application (administering a vaccine) and thus traversed the §101 filter; by contrast, claims that merely collect and compare known information (abstract principle) failed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding preemption concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility analysis considers whether the claim preempts all applications of an idea or is narrowly drawn to a specific implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts emphasize that claims should not 'attempt to preempt every application' of an idea. Bascom and Amdocs stressed that claims limited to particular architectures or ordered combinations that do not preempt all approaches can be eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to natural laws or natural phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely claim a natural law, natural phenomenon, or newly discovered natural relationship can be treated as patent-ineligible unless recited application adds significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges criticized Mayo for discounting 'post-solution activity that is purely conventional or obvious.' Some judges argue inventive concept can arise from application of a natural discovery, while others find overbreadth or lack of inventive concept renders such claims ineligible. Example: Ariosa/Sequenom disputes over claims claiming natural correlations vs. application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overbreadth and §112 as alternative filter
rubrics_metrics.description: Overbroad claims may be problematic under §101, but some judges propose resolving such problems under §112 (indefiniteness/written description) rather than by deeming them ineligible under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Lourie suggested the 'fine filter of §112' may be better suited to treating claims that 'may be indefinite or too broad' rather than exclusion under poorly-defined eligibility rules (Ariosa concurrence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requisites under TRIPS / general patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Per TRIPS Article 27(1), patents must be available for inventions in all fields of technology provided they satisfy other basic conditions: novelty, inventive step/non-obviousness, and industrial applicability/utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an international baseline for WTO members (including the U.S.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public policy/morality and environmental exceptions (TRIPS Article 27(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Members may exclude inventions from patentability if commercial exploitation would be necessary to protect ordre public or morality, including to protect human, animal or plant life or health or to avoid serious prejudice to the environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such exclusions must not be made merely because exploitation is prohibited by law. This provides countries flexibility for moral/public policy exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorical exclusions permitted by TRIPS (Article 27(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: TRIPS permits members to exclude certain subject matter from patent eligibility such as: plants and animals (other than microorganisms); diagnostic, therapeutic, and surgical methods for the treatment of humans or animals; and essentially biological processes for production of plants or animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows explicit carve-outs for specific technology areas at national level while remaining TRIPS-compliant.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPC Article 52 standards and 'as such' exclusions (Europe)
rubrics_metrics.description: European patents are granted for inventions that are new, involve an inventive step, and are susceptible of industrial application; Article 52(2) lists subject matter not regarded as inventions (discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods, aesthetic creations, schemes/rules/methods for mental acts, games, business methods, programs for computers, presentations of information) — excluded 'as such'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the EPC, the 'as such' limitation is key: inventions that apply these abstract categories in a technical manner may still be patentable. EPC Implementing Regulations and EPO practice interpret these exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPC Article 53 public-order and medical exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: EPC Article 53 excludes inventions whose commercial exploitation would be contrary to ordre public or morality; also excludes plant/animal varieties and essentially biological processes; Article 53(c) lists methods for treatment by surgery or therapy and diagnostic methods practiced on the human or animal body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPC practice (EPO Enlarged Board/Technical Boards) has interpreted diagnostic-method exclusion narrowly: only methods that include all steps necessary for a medical (clinical) diagnosis fall within the exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO diagnostic-methods test (clinical-diagnosis step requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is a diagnostic method under Article 53(c) only if it includes all steps necessary for a medical (clinical) diagnosis; methods that merely acquire data or perform in vitro processing without yielding a clinical diagnosis may be patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO Enlarged Board (G 0001/04) and Technical Boards applied this test; examples of eligible claims include methods determining ear temperature or imaging an artery, and in vitro diagnostic steps or software-only processing that do not lead to a clinical conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional approach to diagnostics (Japan/Korea/China)
rubrics_metrics.description: Japan, Korea, and China generally exclude certain diagnostic/therapeutic methods when they are medical in nature, but recognize method claims that do not lead to a medical or clinical diagnosis (e.g., data acquisition or in vitro steps) as potentially patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JPO, KIPO, and SIPO guidelines treat preparatory or separable analytical steps performed outside the body as industrially applicable; China permits methods that obtain intermediate treatment information rather than final diagnostic results to be eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definitions excluding non-technical subject matter (Japan/Korea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Japan and Korea statutorily define 'invention' as a 'highly advanced creation of technical ideas utilizing the laws of nature,' excluding uses of non-natural laws (economics/business), arbitrary arrangements, mathematical formulae, and mental activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner guidelines (JPO, KIPO) elaborate that such non-technical subject matter is not patent-eligible, and Article 32 (Japan) / Article 32 (Korea) permit exclusions for inventions contrary to public order/morality/public health.

rubrics_metrics.name: China's patent exclusions (statutory)
rubrics_metrics.description: China's Patent Act defines invention as new technical solutions for a product/process; it precludes inventions that violate law or social ethics or harm public interests, and specifically excludes scientific discoveries, rules/methods for intellectual activities, methods for diagnosis or treatment of diseases, and animal/plant varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SIPO Guidelines elaborate practice (e.g., allowing intermediate, non-final diagnostic-step claims and conditions for biological material patenting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of naturally occurring substances when isolated/characterized
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdictions often exclude naturally occurring products in their natural form but allow patenting of biological material 'isolated from its natural environment' or produced by technical process, subject to characterization and industrial applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EU Biotechnology Directive affirms patentability of isolated biological material. SIPO allows gene/DNA fragments if: (1) isolated/extracted for first time from nature; (2) structure/morphology/parameters unknown in prior art; (3) can be definitely characterized; (4) can be exploited industrially. Japan/Korea similarly permit artificially isolated substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility of in vitro and data-processing diagnostic steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps performed outside the human body (in vitro), or software-based processing of diagnostic data that do not themselves produce a clinical diagnosis, are often considered patent-eligible across multiple jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO Technical Board and national offices have found such steps patent eligible where they are separable from medical practice; examples include in vitro analysis of tissue/fluid and software programs that perform technical processing rather than yielding a clinical decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-specific examples emphasizing technical character
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts rely on claim-specific factual findings about whether the claim embodies a technical improvement or specific laboratory/technical steps to find eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from Federal Circuit: Rapid Litigation/CellzDirect (cryopreserving hepatocytes = new laboratory technique; eligible), McRO (automatic lip-sync animation = improvement rendering information into specific format), Research Corp. (halftone image rendering = 'functional and palpable' application). These illustrate how factual technical features can carry claims through §101 analysis.
